newsitem.title: UK: Oxford Economic sees no quick upturn in China.
newsitem.headline: Oxford Economic sees no quick upturn in China.

text.p: A relaxation in Chinese monetary policy after two years of austerity for the remainder of 1996 and 1997 will not cause a strong cyclical upturn in the economy, Oxford Economic Forecasting said in its Autumn report.
Gross domestic product growth has slowed to 9.8 percent in the first half of 1996 and retail price inflation to 7.1 percent as the government has achieved its soft landing for the economy.

"Policy-makers are being extremely cautious about relaxing credit controls and their grip over investment growth, as the macroecnomic situation is still delicate, inflationary pressures still substantial," the think-tank said.
Oxford Economic is forecasting GDP growth of 10 percent for the whole of 1996 after 10.2 percent in 1995 and this will rise to 10.9 percent in 1997 and 11.8 percent in 1998.
It notes that state-owned enterprises (SOEs) have encountered more financial difficulties and have rising inter-firm debts.
SOEs made a total loss of 32 billion yuan in the January to March period.

"The government is thus facing difficult policy choices, almost half of the SOEs are suffering losses and the triangle-debt among firms increased by 16.4 percent in the year to the end of the first half of 1996," Oxford Economic said.
It says that while the long-term survival of the SOEs depends on further reforms, many require an injection of credit right now as some cannot pay their workers.
"But too much monetary relaxation would rekindle inflation, which has finally curbed after two-and-half year's of austerity," the report said.
The government cut interest rates in late August for the second time this year as inflation fell from 14.4 percent in 1995.
Oxford Economic sees year-end retail price inflation at 9.2 percent, rising to 10.8 percent in 1997 and 1998.
One bright side of the Chinese economy is the continued high leve of foreign investment, mostly direct investment rather than portfolio flows.
Foreign investment rose 20 percent in the first half of this year to $20 billion and Oxford Economic believes that it will hit $40 billion for the whole of 1996.
